paper.title: Temporal Complexity Hierarchies in Solvable Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
paper.abstract: The influence matrix (IM) provides a powerful framework for characterizing nonequilibrium quantum many-body dynamics by encoding multitime correlations into tensor-network states. Understanding how its computational complexity relates to underlying dynamics is crucial for both theoretical insight and practical utility yet remains largely unexplored despite a few case studies. Here, we address this question for a family of brickwork quantum circuits ranging from integrable to chaotic regimes. Using tools from geometric group theory, we identify three qualitatively distinct scalings of temporal entanglement entropy, establishing a hierarchy of computational resources required for accurate tensor-network representations of the IM for these models. We further analyze the memory structure of the IM and distinguish between classical and quantum temporal correlations. In particular, for certain examples, we identify effectively classical IMs that admit an efficient Monte Carlo algorithm for computing multitime correlations. In more generic settings without an explicit classical description of the IM, we introduce an operational measure of quantum memory with an experimental protocol and discuss examples exhibiting long-time genuinely quantum correlations. Our results establish a new connection between quantum many-body dynamics and group theory, providing fresh insights into the complexity of the IM and its intricate connection to the physical characteristics of the dynamics.

paper.title: Selective aromatization of polyolefins by temporal decoupling from cracking
Post-pandemic immunity debt and environmental decoupling reshape urban influenza transmission
Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
paper.abstract: The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements. Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition. For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$. We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.

paper.title: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
paper.abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security. However, an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12~km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator (LLO) architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of $1.421$~Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and $0.364$~Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario. These results establish an experimental baseline for the performance--complexity trade-off associated with unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.

paper.title: Efficient computation of PEPS gradients for optimized quantum state preparation on 2D topologies
paper.abstract: Quantum state preparation is a fundamental subroutine for quantum computation. For complex, entangled initial states it is, however, difficult to prepare shallow quantum circuits approximating the state with sufficient accuracy. Tensor networks provide a promising avenue of synthesis of such circuits, but most approaches employ 1D Matrix Products States, which struggle to accurately express entangled states in higher dimensions. Here we present a hardware topology-aware quantum state preparation method based on gradient optimization of 2D projected entangled pair states (PEPS). Our approach combines local disentanglement, with global fine tuning based on PEPS gradient optimization. Towards this end we describe an efficient procedure for PEPS gradient computation. We test the convergence and performance of our method in numerical simulations.

paper.title: Noise robust super-Heisenberg scaling in time-dependent quantum sensing by subspace-twirled dynamical decoupling
paper.abstract: In quantum parameter estimation, time-dependent Hamiltonians can enable ultraprecise estimates of a physical parameter beyond the standard Heisenberg limit, also called the super-Heisenberg limit. However, achieving optimal scaling of the measurement precision typically requires an adaptive quantum control scheme which is resource-intensive and hard to implement in general. Furthermore, this advantage is often severely eroded by environmental noise. We propose the use of a dynamical decoupling scheme based on subspace twirling -- the averaging of random unitaries over a subspace rather than the entire Hilbert space -- to overcome these two limitations. We first prove necessary and sufficient conditions for subspace twirling to preserve the encoding signal while simultaneously removing environmental noise. We then establish conditions and provide performance guarantees for when time dependent Hamiltonians undergoing subspace twirling can achieve super-Heisenberg scaling without adaptive controls. Finally, we illustrate our results using an explicit example where a qubit sensor undergoing a subspace twirl simultaneously suppresses noise and achieves super-Heisenberg scaling. These results offer guidance for the design of ultraprecise quantum sensors under time-dependent and noisy conditions.

paper.title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
paper.abstract: We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise. Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values. We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.

paper.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak
paper.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

paper.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak
paper.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

paper.title: Learning to control and predict light-driven electron-phonon dynamics
paper.abstract: Driving lattice vibrations provides a direct route to manipulating electronic correlations through nonlinear electron-phonon coupling. Finding suitable driving fields, however, requires control over the coupled dynamics beyond a simple choice of pulse amplitude and frequency. Here we develop a differentiable framework that combines field optimization with neural-network prediction in a two-site electron-phonon model. We compare piecewise-constant, B-spline, feed-forward, and recurrent control parameterizations, optimized to increase the accumulated electronic double occupation. For the dissipation-free model at zero Hubbard interaction, all the methods increase double occupation, with the B-spline raising the mean total double occupation of approximately 30%. Alongside control optimization, a separate recurrent network learns to predict the next-step double occupation and phonon observables from their preceding values and the applied field. These results establish a computational proof of concept for shaping local electronic correlations through a phonon drive and identify a promising route toward learned models for nonequilibrium materials control.

paper.title: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction
paper.abstract: Continuous quantum error correction promises reduced thresholds and hardware overhead compared to the digital paradigm, but its complex model estimation has greatly reduced its practicality. We recast this problem as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy made of an exact bilinear reduced model, an exact conditional filter, and standard estimation and feedback design. For any $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and which is driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, we prove that the exact filter closes at dimension $3\cdot2^{\,n-k-1}$. This dimension is set by the syndrome space instead of the Hilbert space and is minimal within invariant-subspace filtering. The reduced model exposes and corrects two failure mechanisms of the feedback loop. Strong monitoring damps the rotational partner through which the controller steers the stabilizer and injects back-action diffusion along the recovery path; lowering the measurement strength during correction raises the entanglement fidelity of partner-steering LQR control by $0.096$ in the three-qubit code with three monitored parities. Linearizing at the codespace leaves the syndrome uncontrollable, so the controller can stall; a gain designed at a shifted operating point removes this degeneracy. In the limit of zero measurement during correction, we prove that a syndrome-only filter is exact at every recovery boundary. The resulting committed-recovery controller needs only $2^{\,n-k}$ class probabilities and gives the highest entanglement fidelity compared among the methods tested in the literature, $0.947$ against $0.920$ for a measurement-based estimator protocol in the three-qubit bit-flip code, and $0.726$ vs at most $0.407$ for continuous controllers in the five-qubit perfect code.

paper.title: Ground-State Spin Squeezing and Collective Excitations in $\mathbb{Z}_2$-Symmetric Systems
paper.abstract: Ground-state spin squeezing is a resource for quantum-enhanced measurements, but is commonly associated with a closing excitation gap near a quantum critical point. A closing gap can complicate state preparation and reduce thermal robustness. Here we identify the physical mechanism linking squeezing to collective excitations and establish when stronger squeezing accompanies a larger many-body gap. Using the anisotropic Lipkin--Meshkov--Glick model, we show that, for a quadratic collective mode, the ratio of two transverse fluctuation costs determines squeezing, whereas their geometric mean sets the collective gap. The pair terms responsible for unequal costs are allowed, but not guaranteed, by $\mathbb Z_2$ parity. To extend this picture beyond a single mode, we derive an exact relation between squeezing, polarization, and excitation energies weighted by their collective-spin transition strengths. For XXZ chains, weak-coupling and spin-wave analyses explain how squeezing can develop while both the collective and many-body gaps increase. Exact finite-size calculations for power-law interactions, including the nearest-neighbor limit, confirm a negative-coupling branch on which the two gaps coincide and increase as squeezing improves. For nearest-neighbor interactions, this branch also retains squeezing at higher temperatures than a gap-closing branch with comparable ground-state squeezing. In the Ising chain, by contrast, a staggered excitation can lower the many-body gap without directly contributing to collective fluctuations. Our results explain why ground-state squeezing can accompany either a closing or an opening collective gap, and identify a gap-opening branch with enhanced thermal robustness and the potential for faster adiabatic preparation.

paper.title: Persistent-mediator architecture for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation with color codes
paper.abstract: Two-dimensional color codes provide transversal Clifford gates, whereas suitable three-dimensional codes provide a transversal $T$ gate. Representative cross-dimensional schemes either switch the computational encoding or consume a 3D encoded state. Reusing the same protected 3D block would remove repeated auxiliary-state preparation and terminal readout, raising a central question: can the 3D module remain encoded and protected while mediating successive $T$ gates on a separate 2D register? Here we introduce a cross-dimensional persistent-mediator architecture that retains the 2D data register and 3D mediator as distinct encoded modules at each cycle boundary, coupled only through a transient protected subsystem. We construct a membrane-like joint-logical measurement and combine it with a matched cross-dimensional $CZ$, complementary string-like surgery, and feed-forward to close a deterministic logical $T$-gate cycle. The cycle avoids post-selection and destructive mediator readout and restores the 3D block to its initial logical state. Stabilizer analysis establishes the logical action and preserved spatial distance. Phenomenological and circuit-level simulations of a Clifford surrogate show finite-distance scaling close to the matched 3D memory benchmark, while sequential tests show approximately linear logical-error accumulation in the low-error regime. Persistent mediation enables repeated access to higher-dimensional non-Clifford capability while keeping the computational register in its 2D encoding.

paper.title: Asymptotic Attainability of the Channel RLD Fisher-Information Bound
paper.abstract: The channel right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information is a computable upper bound on the optimal asymptotic symmetric-logarithmic-derivative (SLD) Fisher information per channel use over causally ordered, parameter-independent strategies. The bound is not always attained, even if the Choi matrix is positive definite. We determine exactly when equality holds using a semidefinite feasibility condition involving only the Choi matrix and its first derivative. The condition allows a degenerate largest eigenvalue of the RLD matrix and rank-deficient Choi matrices with derivatives supported on their range. The original channel family may change rank nearby. For generalized dephasing channels with a positive-definite correlation matrix at the evaluation point, the condition becomes a system of linear equations for nonnegative certificate weights that sum to one. At a completely dephasing point we also calculate the optimal SLD information for every finite number of uses and show that a repeated, ancilla-free probe attains it, even against adaptive strategies. Explicit examples give an unbounded ratio of the channel RLD information to the optimal asymptotic SLD information per use, either as the dimension grows or at fixed qubit dimension as the smallest Choi eigenvalue tends to zero. We derive the equality criterion and its consequences from the asymptotic optimization of Zhou and Jiang.

paper.title: Quantum Mpemba effect from logical-information exposure in monitored circuits
paper.abstract: In the Mpemba effect, a state initially farther from stationarity overtakes one that starts closer. After one cycle in a monitored Clifford chain, an unencoded Bell-pair state has lower mean entanglement entropy than a scrambled reference prepared from fewer pairs. The gap grows linearly with chain length. This reversal is driven by logical-information exposure: a stabilizer state loses one ebit per independent logical parity resolved by the record. Scrambling within each half can spread this information over many sites while preserving every Schmidt coefficient. We prove that with independent exact unitary two-design encoders, any pure reference ensemble with no greater mean initial entropy can lead in mean entropy by at most two ebits at any time. If the stationary entropy is subextensive, the unencoded reversal is a quantum Mpemba effect at large sizes. We further certify this effect at 128 and 256 qubits using stationary-entropy bounds.

paper.title: Circuit-Level Analysis of Quantum Error Correction in Second-Generation Quantum Repeaters
paper.abstract: We present a circuit-level simulation of second-generation quantum repeaters with stabilizer-based quantum error correction. We model a two-segment repeater link including encoding, syndrome extraction, decoding, and entanglement swapping, and compare the performance of the single-error-correcting Steane and five-qubit stabilizer codes under different noise scenarios. To that extent, we consider noise sources with incoherent (depolarizing and dephasing) and coherent (systematic over-rotation) errors and incorporate them directly at the circuit level. While the Steane code outperforms the five-qubit code at coherent errors, the five-qubit code achieves higher end-to-end fidelities under incoherent noise in the low-noise regime when a large number of physical qubits is affected by it. At higher noise regimes, employing no code turns out to be the best option. In mixed noise scenarios, we observe moderate cross-effects between the noise classes regarding the error correction performance. We conclude that code selection in second-generation quantum repeaters must be adapted to the dominant physical noise mechanism and that circuit complexity and hardware-aware implementation options influence performance in coherent-error-dominated regimes, providing design insights for error correction in quantum repeaters.

paper.title: Scaling Pêlagos: Multi-GPU Orchestration for Relay Belief-Propagation Decoding
paper.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum error-correction (QEC) decoders that achieve low logical error rates under real-time operating constraints. These constraints motivate heuristic decoding algorithms whose error-correction performance must be evaluated through large-scale simulation. High-throughput decoding accelerates this evaluation and the exploration of decoder parameters. Using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs) is a natural way to scale these simulations, but naively distributing syndrome batches introduces host-side preprocessing and output-collection overheads that limit scaling. To address these limitations, we extend the Pêlagos relay belief-propagation (Relay-BP) decoder with process-isolated orchestration, parallel host preprocessing, and shared-memory output. We evaluate both one-gross ($[[144,12,12]]$) and two-gross ($[[288,12,18]]$) codes in a multi-GPU environment. Specifically, for the one-gross circuit at $R=50$, eight AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs achieve optimized end-to-end speedups of $5.68\times$ and $6.23\times$, respectively. For the two-gross circuit, the corresponding speedups are $6.92\times$ and $7.01\times$. When throughput is calculated using GPU decoding time, the corresponding two-gross speedups are $7.58\times$ and $7.45\times$, indicating near-linear GPU scaling. We deploy Pêlagos on Lux, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's AMD Instinct MI355X-based supercomputer, as a pathfinding application for high-throughput QEC simulation. This deployment provides a concrete quantum-computing use case for the AI + HPC infrastructure supporting the Genesis Mission's scientific-discovery goals. These end-to-end measurements demonstrate a practical path to accelerating large-scale QEC simulation through efficient multi-GPU decoding.

paper.title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
paper.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

paper.title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
paper.abstract: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.

paper.title: Hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits for stabilizer codes
paper.abstract: Quantum error correction is the art of protecting fragile quantum information through suitable encoding and active interventions. However, it is notoriously difficult to manipulate encoded quantum data without causing uncorrectable errors. Here, we introduce a mathematical framework for constructing hardware-tailored circuits that implement any desired Clifford unitary on the logical level of any given stabilizer code. We formulate this task as a discrete optimization problem that minimizes the number of CZ gates while naturally incorporating a parameterization of all Clifford stabilizers. Despite the intrinsic difficulty of the circuit compilation problem, our methods scale to at least 16 physical qubits. Because our circuits require very few CZ gates, they provide excellent starting points for constructing fault-tolerant implementations using flag gadgets. Using a brute-force search, we develop several such flag gadgets, including weakly fault-tolerant logical Hadamard circuits for the [[8, 3, 2]] code that require an unprecedentedly small number of physical two-qubit gates. Our work introduces both the mathematics and software for compiling hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits. From a broader perspective, we turn away from the standard generator decomposition and instead focus on the holistic compilation of entire logical circuits, leading to significant savings in practice.

paper.title: Phase Interference and Transverse Catalysts Govern the Noise Fragility of Long-Range Variational Quantum Circuits
paper.abstract: Long-range entangling gates shorten variational state preparation, but they also accelerate operator spreading across the register, linking nonlocality to a presumed noise fragility. Here we show that the single-fault fragility $F$ of a variational circuit is governed by how fault phases interfere on the target Hamiltonian, not by how far faults spread. For Heisenberg chains we prove that two faults with identical extensive support can incur either bounded or extensive energy damage, in the exact ratio $N/2$. A phase-matched longitudinal halo remains energetically dark until ignited by transverse catalysts that break a symmetry of the remote register, namely spatially nonuniform single-qubit rotations or the pair-flip component of two-qubit $XX/YY$ gates, whereas uniform rotations and magnetization-conserving exchange gates leave it strictly dark. In noisy training with full-width long-range $ZZ$ gates, suppressing either catalyst alone leaves circuits trapped on an ignited plateau sustained by remote $XY$ couplings, whereas suppressing both eliminates the plateau, achieves minimal fragility despite larger fault operators, and halves the dephasing error. Training is driven by a race between catalyst pruning and gradient force balance, as annealing the transverse catalysts out of trapped circuits rescues every trajectory while annealing the entire longitudinal sector does not. Combined with the gate-count exposure $λ=pK$, a single fragility measurement accurately predicts the noise-induced energy shift across circuit architectures and noise strengths, reducing ansatz design to a trade-off between coherent expressivity and gate count.

paper.title: Quasi-Cyclic Qudit Lifted Product Codes with Almost Linear Minimum Distance
paper.abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are a promising route to fault-tolerant quantum computation with low overhead, and qudits offer advantages over qubits including more efficient information representation, improved magic state distillation, and richer algebraic structure for code design. Asymptotically good QLDPC codes arise from the lifted product (LP) construction with non-abelian lifts, but cyclic lifts remain attractive in practice because the resulting quasi-cyclic codes have circulant structure that hardware decoders exploit, which matters especially for non-binary decoders with costly check node operations. We introduce a qudit generalization of the LP construction over cyclic group algebras, which extends hypergraph product and LP codes to arbitrary prime-power dimensions and yields quasi-cyclic qudit CSS codes for every stacking order. We bound encoding rates via a connection to additive codes, and show that in the fully stacked case, qudit LP codes built from lifted Tanner codes on expander graphs form families with $Θ(\log N)$ logical qudits and almost linear minimum distance $Θ(N/\log N)$, via a distance bound that holds for a general class of LP factors. We also study an additive decoder for general qudit codes and a linear merged-syndrome decoder for fully stacked codes. Monte Carlo simulations under a depolarizing channel with equal symbol error probability show that qudit codes achieve lower frame error rates than comparable qubit codes, and that the linear decoder gives further gains for fully stacked codes.

paper.title: Enhanced Entanglement Gate Fidelity via Correlated and Synchronized Atom Motion
paper.abstract: Engineered collective dissipation can correlate and even synchronize the motion of quantum systems. We show that such motional correlations can suppress motion-induced errors in two-qubit controlled-phase gates based on the Rydberg blockade in neutral-atom tweezer arrays. To leading order in the Lamb-Dicke parameter, the motional contribution to the gate infidelity is determined solely by the two-atom motional occupations and correlations, and is independent of the gate protocol. We illustrate this result for correlated thermal states and synchronized quantum van der Pol oscillators. In each case, motional correlations reduce the gate infidelity relative to independent thermal atoms at finite temperature. Our results establish atomic-motion correlations as a resource for high-fidelity neutral-atom gates and may also find applications in analog quantum simulators.

paper.title: Statistical-to-computational gaps in central limit theorems for high-dimensional tensors
paper.abstract: We study high-dimensional central limit theorems (CLTs) as hypothesis testing problems, comparing the number of summands needed for statistical and computational indistinguishability of the normalized sum from the limiting Gaussian distribution as the dimension and number of summands grow together. For the off-diagonal entries of sums of i.i.d. rank-one tensors formed from standard Gaussian vectors (equivalently, the problem of distinguishing Wigner from Wishart tensors), we prove total variation bounds sharpening previous estimates of Mikulincer (2020) and give matching polynomial-time tests. This shows that the statistical and computational thresholds coincide for this CLT, contrary to a proposal by Kunisky, Moore, and Wein (2024). On the other hand, we also show that, for tensors of order at least three, sufficient Gaussian dilution of the summands by adding independent Gaussian noise and rescaling gives a CLT model with a statistical-to-computational gap (in the above setting and ones with more general rank-one summand distributions). To the best of our knowledge, such a phenomenon has not been observed before in any high-dimensional CLT. In particular, in the relevant parameter regimes, we show that a brute-force search achieves strong detection, while polynomials of degree up to $n^{Ω(1)}$ cannot achieve strong separation. The latter lower bounds control low-degree $χ^2$-divergences by a novel method based on cumulant generating functions, and we further illustrate the use of these tools by applying them to masked tensor CLT models where only a prescribed subset of tensor entries is revealed.

paper.title: On Multi-Constrained Path Finding utilizing Grover Search and Decoded Quantum Interferometry
paper.abstract: Finding a path whose totals under several additive metrics all fall inside prescribed ranges is weakly NP-complete. We ask what two quantum algorithms can do for it, against strong classical baselines. For directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) we give a Grover search whose state preparation builds the uniform superposition over all source-to-destination paths with one qubit per arc and no ancilla. We prove it correct, give its exact gate count, and show that measured strings form an error- detecting code whose distance is a girth-like graph parameter. We complete the oracle and count its gates: one search on our largest instance, 136 arc qubits and 262,144 paths, needs about 4.4 x 10^5 Toffoli gates, while classical dynamic programming decides the same instance with 18,754 labels. Grover search needs O(sqrt(N/M)) oracle calls for M good paths among N . Classical meet-in-the-middle matches this exponent in the worst case, and known quantum algorithms with quantum memory beat it. For a staged fabric with node-independent linear weights, maximizing the number of satisfied metrics is max-LINSAT, and with power- of-index weights it is Optimal Polynomial Intersection, where no known polynomial-time classical algorithm matches decoded quantum interferometry (DQI). We verify this translation in simulation and run two small binary instances on IBM Heron processors, which keep 67 % and 15 % of the ideal gain over uniform sampling.

paper.title: Feedback Control and Neural-Network-Based Prediction of Quantum Entanglement in Fano-mirror cavity optomechanics
paper.abstract: Quantum entanglement involving the centre-of-mass motion of macroscopic-scale objects plays an essential role in both fundamental science and emerging quantum technologies, yet generating and verifying such macroscopic nonclassical states remain formidable challenges. Here, we report a theoretical scheme to effectively generate, manipulate, and predict bipartite optomechanical entanglement based on a Fano-mirror cavity optomechanical system with a coherent feedback loop, where the cavity and Fano optical modes couple through coherent and dissipative interactions. We show that the Fano mirror forms a closed tripartite interaction loop with the cavity and mechanical modes, whereby the quantum interference between direct and indirect interaction pathways substantially enhances the cavity-mechanical entanglement and gives rise to a robust Fano-mechanical entanglement. More importantly, we find that coherent feedback combined with an appropriate optical frequency mismatch can further enhance the entanglement, and a trained supervised feedforward neural network can be used to predict the entanglement magnitude from the readily measurable optical signals, relaxing the requirement of full quantum-state tomography. Our work, establishing an all-optical and experimentally feasible approach to generate, manipulate, and characterize the macroscopic optomechanical entanglement, holds great potential for applications in quantum information processing.

paper.title: VR-Net: Subarray-Level Inter-Cell Coordination for Multi-Cell XL-MIMO under Near-Field Spatial Non-Stationarity
paper.abstract: Spatial non-stationarity in multi-cell extremely large-scale MIMO (XL-MIMO) confines each user to a visibility region (VR) of each array. VR-Net exploits these regions for subarray-level coordinated beamforming. A base-station (BS)-indexed conflict graph identifies overlapping VRs; gain-based association and a masked multi-cell weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) iteration restrict beam design and channel state information (CSI) uploads to the relevant subarray blocks. We establish conditions for exact per-cell decoupling, derive the expected CSI loads, bound the loss of designing on the VR-gated channel and the loss of the support constraint, and characterize single-edge visibility contrast through a closed-form Fresnel transition width. Simulations use a 3GPP TR 38.901 Release-19-based near-field UMi channel with modular facade arrays and pre-registered criteria. At a 30 dB threshold, VR-Net retains at least 99.6% of the full-aperture WMMSE sum rate in every tested setting while uploading 10-39% fewer complex CSI entries. It gains up to 3.5 bit/s/Hz over an all-user adaptation of the multi-cell scheme of Pérez-Adán et al. at moderate power and dense load, and inter-cell coordination adds up to 33% over per-cell design.

paper.title: A Unified Benchmarking Study of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Ansatz for Electronic Structure Problems
paper.abstract: Electronic structure calculations become computationally expensive on classical computers as electron correlation increases. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative through hybrid quantum-classical Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) on Noisy-Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. The choice of ansatz plays a pivotal role in the performance and scalability of the VQE, yet selecting an optimal ansatz remains challenging. Existing approaches including chemically inspired ansatz, adaptive schemes and Hardware Efficient Ansätze (HEA) lack a unified comparison. This gap makes the scalability and trade-offs of each method unclear for varying molecular sizes. This work presents a systematic benchmarking study comparing Unitary Couples Cluster Singles and Doubles Ansatz (UCCSD), fermionic ADAPT-VQE, BasicPCA HEA, and Excitation Preserving HEA across molecules of varying size like $H_2$, $LiH$, $N_2$. We evaluate trade-offs among circuit depth, parameter count, ground-state energy error, and NISQ feasibility. ADAPT-VQE achieves accuracy comparable to UCCSD with lower resource overhead, but becomes impractical for modest system sizes ($\sim$10 electrons) due to increasing circuit complexity. In contrast, HEA reduces hardware costs but requires more parameters and sacrifices accuracy, with performance strongly dependent on molecular size. The Excitation Preserving ansatz remains below chemical accuracy for $H_2$ and $LiH$, and fails for $N_2$, underscoring the need to balance expressibility and trainability. Overall, these results highlight key trade-offs between accuracy and resource efficiency across VQE ansätze, emphasizing the need to improve ADAPT-VQE scalability and HEA accuracy while addressing optimization challenges for near-term quantum hardware.

paper.title: Multimodal Semantic Communication using Shared and Unique Representation Decomposition
paper.abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm for bandwidth-constrained mobile and vehicular networks. This paper proposes a unified representation learning framework for multimodal SemCom (MSC), which encodes heterogeneous data into a compact semantic space for efficient transmission and source recovery. The framework addresses the multimodal semantic representation gap, which arises when at least one modality contains semantic information that cannot be fully inferred from the other. To preserve this information for reconstruction, the framework decomposes each representation into shared and modality-specific components. We formulate a mutual information objective for source reconstruction, cross-modal alignment of the shared components, and decoupling of the shared and modality-specific components. To enhance transmission efficiency, we introduce a shared knowledge base implemented as a compact codebook of semantic vectors learned during training. The shared components are transmitted digitally as codebook indices, while the modality-specific components are sent in analog form. We apply knowledge distillation during training, using a pretrained vision foundation model to guide the learning of quantized shared features. On image--text pairs over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Extended Vehicular A (EVA) channels, the proposed framework improves image reconstruction over conventional separate source-channel coding (SSCC) and representative multimodal and unimodal SemCom systems. Further evaluations show gradual degradation under channel-estimation mismatch, complementary effects of alignment, decoupling, and knowledge distillation on the shared representation, and alignment of shared features across modalities with separation of the modality-specific features.

paper.title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures for Financial Time Series Prediction
paper.abstract: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.

paper.title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
paper.abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

paper.title: An Architecture for Real-Time Quantum Error Correction with Neutral Atoms
paper.abstract: The latency of quantum measurement and classical decoding constrains the execution of adaptive fault-tolerant circuits. In neutral-atom processors, this requirement couples spatially resolved fluorescence detection to classical inference. Here we implement cascaded readout and decoding in a heterogeneous architecture that overlaps acquisition and processing at two spatial scales. Field-programmable gate arrays process camera rows as they arrive, while graphics processors decode an acquired logical block during acquisition of the next. This heterogeneous architecture offers flexibility in the choice of error-correcting codes and decoding algorithms. Direct communication preserves microsecond-scale transfer times for kilobyte payloads and supports interchangeable decoding algorithms. Hardware characterization and decoding benchmarks using circuit-level simulated syndromes yield a submillisecond post-exposure processing latency for selected small-code workloads ($d = 3, 5, 7$). By enabling logical blocks to be decoded before full-frame readout is complete, the architecture implements low-latency syndrome decoding, realizing real-time quantum information processing as required for fault-tolerant computation in atom arrays.

paper.title: Scalable Compilation of Resource-Efficient Tapers for High-Confidence Quantum Phase Estimation
paper.abstract: Quantum phase estimation is a key component of many quantum algorithms. Recently, high-confidence, tapered QPE (tQPE) has been introduced, significantly reducing the number of ancilla qubits necessary for a given failure probability, $ε$. We consider tQPE with $p = l+m$ ancillas, where $l$ represents the number of ancillas necessary to estimate a phase to a given resolution and $m$ represents the number of ''confidence'' qubits added to ensure a desired success probability. With tQPE the failure probability decays double exponentially in $m$, implying that only a few confidence qubits suffice for virtually any problem of interest. A key challenge for tQPE is the construction of the quantum circuit for preparing the taper state on the ancilla register. Here, we develop scalable tensor network methods (previous work was limited to ($l + m = 24$)) giving highly optimized state preparation circuits for optimally concentrated DPSS (Slepian) tapers. We provide an accompanying database of resource-efficient state preparation circuits for $l = 1, \dots, 50$ and $m = 1, \dots, 4$. Our circuits are shallow enough for a demonstration on near-term devices for small values of $l$. We run tQPE circuits for a 1-qubit system initialized in the ground state on Quantinuum's H2-2 quantum computer, demonstrating a $3\times$ to $18\times$ reduction in failure probability for $l=1,\ldots,10$ on a noisy device.

paper.title: Time- and Photon-Optimal Paths for the Preparation and Logical Flip of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill States
paper.abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are highly non-Gaussian, making their control challenging, particularly in the presence of photon loss. Here, we use the brachistochrone, the fastest path at bounded speed, to construct ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians for state preparation and logical gates, and compare it with the photon-optimal path. We find that the two paths nearly coincide for state preparation but differ markedly for logical operations, namely the brachistochrone preserves the encoded qubit during a bit flip, whereas the photon-optimal path flips a known state through the vacuum. We then introduce the tangential capacity to quantify how effectively gate sets track these paths. Using this analysis, we find that conditional squeezing achieves the highest capacity, preparing GKP states in 824 ns with a fidelity of 0.99 and a minimum closeness to the path of 0.90, compared with 0.98 and 0.51 for conditional displacements and 0.83 and 0.19 for SNAP gates.

paper.title: Local enhancement of finite-strength code preparation: recoverability and Wilson coherence
paper.abstract: Stabilizer measurements provide a direct route to preparing quantum error-correcting codes and long-range entangled states. In realistic implementations, however, finite measurement strength can coherently deform the encoding map away from the projective limit. Certain nonlocal signatures associated with long-range order can survive such a deformation, but this alone does not guarantee that the resulting state protects encoded quantum information. We show that, at fixed strength, local logical leakage obstructs asymptotically faithful recovery; along logical operators' supports, its accumulation forces the relevant measurement strength to grow logarithmically with code distance. We then prove that this obstruction can be removed locally: for fixed toric registers under sufficiently weak local-stochastic errors, enhancing only a vanishing fraction of checks near selected logical supports restores recovery while the bulk remains at finite measurement strength. With recoverability restored, we prove a further dimensional distinction in logical operations. In the strict three-dimensional deconfined phase, suitable enhanced tubes restore the equivalence of macroscopically separated representatives, so either representative asymptotically implements the same controlled logical action on a fixed encoding. In two dimensions, recoverability alone does not restore this equivalence: the representatives can remain inequivalent even when both associated encodings are recoverable.

paper.title: CSS Circuits: useful quantum circuits that can be simulated with $O(1)$ cost per gate
paper.abstract: "CSS circuits" are quantum circuits generated by $X$, $Z$, $M_X$, $M_Z$, and CNOT gates. Although CSS circuits are extremely restrictive, they can implement important quantum protocols like teleportation, error correction, and entanglement purification. We present a simple CSS circuit simulator that uses $O(1)$ work per gate. The simulator corresponds to a local hidden variable model, so we use Bell inequalities to prove the simulator can't also support Hadamard gates, CZ gates, or S gates. We note that CSS circuits appear ideal for benchmarking quantum error correction in the presence of atom loss errors.

paper.title: Quantum CSS codes: Decoder-aware multiobjective design and bound-certified selection
paper.abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes trade decoding reliability against the resources needed to measure their checks. We formulate Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code design at fixed encoding resources as a decoder-aware multiobjective problem. The objectives are failure probability under sector-wise degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and check weight, the minimum total weight of an independent pure-type generator basis. For independent bit- and phase-flip noise with perfect syndrome extraction, deterministic truncation bounds support selection under a failure-rate constraint. At a per-sector error probability of 0.01, the bounds certify that a code encoding two logical qubits into 40 physical qubits meets a failure-rate target of 0.001 at check weight 139. The lower bound of every cheaper candidate in the corresponding (40,2) main menu exceeds this target. In paired searches sharing one annealing kernel and equal query budgets, decoder-aware guidance gives significantly higher mean final hypervolume than distance guidance in all eight tested configurations under the reported Holm correction. Against distance-multiplicity guidance, five configurations show significant gains and three do not, including one with a negative mean difference. All arms are scored in common truncated-reliability and normalized-check-weight coordinates. The framework connects reliability-check-weight trade-offs to bound-certified selection within evaluated CSS pools.

paper.title: Evaluating Quantum Circuit Protection Methods After Compilation: An Empirical Comparison
paper.abstract: Quantum cloud providers can read the circuits they receive and their outputs, yet methods for hiding a circuit are usually evaluated on the circuit as written, before compilation optimises it. We compare three ObfusQate schemes (inverse, composite and delayed gates), ECQCO and Q-MaskCut under one protocol that compiles every protected circuit at optimisation level 3 before measuring it; the goal is to keep the provider from learning the user's algorithm and answer. Q-MaskCut is one example combination of existing techniques: a one-time-pad key, decoy wires, circuit cutting with a random rotation pair across each cut, and Pauli twirling with dynamical-decoupling masking after compilation. We simulate 11 circuits of 3 to 19 qubits without noise and on two noise models, measure the compiled structure and execution time of 23 circuits of 3 to 127 qubits, and test whether the structural disguise survives a second compilation by the provider. Composite and delayed gates lose most of their structural disguise in compilation and leave the output readable; inverse gates keep a high normalised graph edit distance (normGED) only by making execution 7 to 112 times longer; ECQCO's output could not be decoded with the implementation provided by its authors. Q-MaskCut hides the output (mean total variation distance without the key 0.94), and without noise, with exact fragment probabilities, it decodes exactly. Its compiled normGED of 0.88 comes mostly from the masking, which a second compilation removes, leaving 0.42 from the key, decoys and padlocks. With noise, its fidelity is comparable to the original's; it needs 7 to 91 fragment variants per circuit in the simulations (7 to 61 in a run on ibm_marrakesh) and a classical reconstruction. Protection should therefore be evaluated on the compiled circuit and again after the provider recompiles it.
